clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive HOXA1-spectrum disorder first described in Native American Athabaskan-speaking populations
Horizontal gaze palsy and Duane-type ocular motility restriction reflect abducens pathway maldevelopment
Sensorineural deafness arises from inner ear malformation, as in the related HOXA1 phenotypes
Central hypoventilation is a prominent and potentially dangerous feature
Facial weakness, swallowing difficulty, and developmental delay may be present
Vascular and cardiac anomalies overlap with those of Bosley-Salih-Alorainy syndrome
A common founder HOXA1 variant underlies most cases in the originally described population
Diagnosis is by identification of biallelic HOXA1 variants, often the recurrent founder allele
reference.pathophysiology: Athabaskan brainstem dysgenesis is caused by biallelic HOXA1 variants, frequently a founder allele in the population in which it was first recognised. HOXA1 is a homeobox transcription factor required for correct segmentation and patterning of the embryonic hindbrain into rhombomeres. Deficient HOXA1 activity disrupts the development of brainstem structures that give rise to ocular motor and other cranial nerve pathways, the inner ear, and the neural circuits controlling respiration, alongside the vascular and cardiac derivatives of the region. This shared developmental disturbance produces the combination of horizontal gaze abnormality, deafness, central hypoventilation, and cardiovascular anomalies, distinguishing it from the related Bosley-Salih-Alorainy phenotype partly by population origin and the relative prominence of brainstem dysfunction.

reference.prognosis: The prognosis is chiefly determined by the severity of central hypoventilation and any associated cardiovascular anomaly, which can be life-threatening in infancy; hearing loss and ocular motility limitation are stable and manageable, and with respiratory support and multidisciplinary care survival into later childhood and beyond is possible, though developmental outcome varies.
pitfalls: Failing to investigate respiratory control and missing dangerous central hypoventilation
Interpreting the gaze abnormality in isolation and overlooking the systemic HOXA1 syndrome
Not testing for the recurrent founder variant in individuals of relevant ancestry
Neglecting cardiovascular and carotid imaging in an affected infant

management: Respiratory support for central hypoventilation, ranging from non-invasive ventilation to tracheostomy and assisted ventilation, guided by sleep and ventilation studies
Cardiology and vascular management of associated cardiac and carotid anomalies, informed by echocardiography and vascular imaging
Audiological rehabilitation for sensorineural deafness with hearing aids or cochlear implantation
Feeding and swallowing support with aspiration precautions and gastrostomy where bulbar dysfunction requires it
Developmental and neuro-ophthalmological support for gaze limitation and developmental delay
Multidisciplinary follow-up and genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive HOXA1 disorder, including founder-variant testing and family screening
A clear monitoring and escalation plan for life-threatening apnoea and hypoventilation in infancy
